newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Afghan frontier quiet but Uzbek troops prepare.
newsitem.headline: Afghan frontier quiet but Uzbek troops prepare.

text.p: Soldiers were digging trenches along the Amu Darya river on Tuesday and a solitary Uzbek tank guarded the Friendship Bridge spanning the old Soviet frontier with Afghanistan.

The military activity was evidence of an unease that has gripped all of former Soviet Central Asia and reached as far as the Kremlin following the dramatic advance of the fundamentalist Taleban militia into northern Afghanistan.

Officials from Russia, Uzbekistan and seven other ex-Soviet republics met in Moscow on Tuesday to discuss security in the region. They fear a flood of refugees, including possibly thousands of defeated but still armed anti-Taleban fighters.
So far at Friendship Bridge there has been no sign of an exodus along the Kabul road. "There have been no refugees in the last few days," one aid worker told Reuters on Tuesday.
But Uzbek troops have orders to reinforce the border.

The tank's gun points out over a hastily erected concrete barricade and across the massive bridge over the Amu Darya which carried an invading Soviet army into Afghanistan in 1979 -- and back out again, defeated, 10 years later.

Sixty km (40 miles) down the road lies Mazar-i-Sharif, until Friday the stronghold of ethnic Uzbek commander Abdul Rashid Dostum, a key opponent of the Taleban. Dostum is now in Turkey and Mazar-i-Sharif is firmly in the hands of the Taleban, who are rapidly imposing their strict form of Islam.
"We do not like the Taleban," the Uzbek lieutenant in command of the border post said.

The calm that has held on the frontier since the militia's advance gave him some hope, however, that the Taleban, who are predominantly southerners, would allow Dostum's former ally, Abdul Malik, to control the north. Abdul Malik went over to the Taleban, undermining the opposition alliance.
"The last few days have been quiet, and we hope that if Abdul Malik continues controlling northern Afghanistan the situation will remain stable," the officer said.

In Termez, an Uzbek town of around 100,000, just nine km (six miles) from the bridge the mood was outwardly calm although residents admitted to being worried by the sudden advance of fundamentalist Islam to their doorstep.

The central market -- always a barometer of social life in Central Asia -- was working normally. Stalls were laden with fruit, vegetables and Uzbek candy and sellers noisily proclaimed their wares to lure crowds of visitors.
"I am not afraid of the Taleban, although many in Termez now do," said one of the sellers, offering large, juicy cherries from Samarkand in eastern Uzbekistan.

But in the streets, where there was a noticeably heavy police presence, many said they were alarmed by the news from northern Afghanistan, and especially about the Taleban imposing rigid Islamic rule in Dostum's old territory.
"We learnt about the fall of Mazar-i-Sharif, and many are worried," said Akhmet, a 40-year-old private driver.
Ordinary Uzbeks are mainly Moslems but many share the official view in the capital Tashkent that the Taleban could bring instability.
"This extremism is no good," another driver said.
"My relatives called from Tashkent the day after the fall of Mazar-i-Sharif and asked if my family was planning to escape from the Taleban."
